newsitem.title: USA: Most IMM currency futures end near session lows.
newsitem.headline: Most IMM currency futures end near session lows.

text.p: Most IMM currencies closed near session lows which were set in the last hour of pit trade after a monetary source said to a wire service that the yen's present level does not require intervention, analysts said.
"The quote plays to the market's view on G7 that there doesn't seem to be teeth or commitment to turning the dollar around," Alan Ruskin, director/chief of economics at I.D.E.A. Inc, said.
The wire-service story did not elaborate on the monetary source, who said the yen's level does not reflect any misalignment.
June yen set a contract low at $0.007931, cracking through the previous contract low of $0.007935, as the dollar/yen finally gained upside momentum after a mostly lackluster day.
Even June marks, which rose to $0.5817 or about 1.7250 spot marks earlier in the day, slipped to fresh session lows. June fell to $0.5788, above its contract low at $0.5768.

Until the wire-service story, many short-term traders and pit traders were disappointed by the lack of follow-through activity after dollar rose above or near multi-year highs against the mark and yen in overnight trade.
By the time U.S. dealings began on Monday, the forex market had fully reacted to the G7 communique on Sunday which reiterated that G7 nations would intervene when appropriate.
Comments from various G7 officials on Monday did not offer the market any clues on what the G7 considers appropriate intervention levels.
"We don't know where the pain threshold level is," Marc Chandler, senior analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said. "And to expect them to give specific levels for intervention is unreasonable."
Chandler said the various comments from G-7 officials reinforced the idea that the forex policy change made in Berlin in February 1997 was intact, and that there was still no sense of urgency.
"The threat of intervention might be more important than intervention," Ruskin said.

In addition, the forex market also faces a heavy schedule of U.S. economic reports this week. The first-quarter U.S. employment cost index, which will be released at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT on Tuesday, is expected to rise 0.9 percent, from up 0.8 percent in fourth-quarter 1997.

At the end of pit trade, June yen lost $0.000043 to $0.007933, marks fell $0.0022 to $0.5790, Swiss francs declined $0.0026 to $0.6818, sterling rose $0.0018 to $1.6236, Canadian dollar fell $0.0017 to $0.7167, Aussie dollar rose $0.0031 to $0.7799, Mexican peso slid $0.001375 to $0.122400.
